analysis.one_liner: Bans large online platforms from using deceptive design and running unconsented behavioral experiments on users.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the House and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The DETOUR Act would have barred any online service with more than 100 million users from designing its interface to trick people into giving up personal data or consent, or into compulsive use. It would have required companies to get clear, informed consent before running psychological or behavioral experiments on users, to disclose such research every 90 days, and to set up independent review boards to approve the studies. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: The hundreds of millions of people who use large social media and other online services. The bill would have curbed "dark patterns" — interface tricks like hard-to-cancel subscriptions, misleading buttons, and endless auto-play — and would have ended the practice of quietly experimenting on users to steer their behavior without telling them, which on these platforms means most internet users in the country.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of large social media platforms

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for a large online operator to design its interface with the purpose or effect of impairing user autonomy or choice in order to extract consent or personal data [S3].
It requires informed consent before any behavioral or psychological experiment or research on users, and counts minors under 18 as unable to give that consent themselves [S3].

It bans designs that cultivate compulsive usage, including auto-playing video without clear consent, and bans designs aimed at minors under 18 that increase their use of social platforms without parental consent [S3].

It obligates any operator running behavioral research to disclose it to affected users at least every 90 days, stop studies with improperly obtained consent, and create an FTC-registered independent review board to approve or veto the studies [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large online operators — social networks and other platforms with over 100 million users — would bear the cost of redesigning their products, disclosing and restricting their behavioral research, and funding independent review boards. Indirectly, that cost would fall on the advertising-driven business model of those platforms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large online platforms and their advertisers

drawbacks.text: The rules would reach ordinary product testing: the bill's ban covers any interface change whose purpose or substantial effect is to impair user choice, and the FTC would have to write exemptions for routine layout and style tests [S3].
The 100-million-user threshold exempts every smaller website and app, leaving users of those services with no protection from the same practices [S3].
Terms like "compulsive usage" and "impairing user autonomy" are broad, which could invite slow FTC rulemaking and litigation rather than quick changes to how products are built [S3].
Requiring an independent review board for every behavioral study would impose real compliance costs on large platforms, costs that could be passed on or simply slow feature development [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections would touch nearly every user of the largest online services, at a cost concentrated on a handful of platform companies whose business models depend on maximizing engagement and data collection. The main honest objection is design: the threshold leaves smaller platforms unregulated and the broad language could make enforcement slow and litigated. But the bill never got far enough for those issues to be worked out in committee.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced it two weeks before the session ended, no one cosponsored it, the Energy and Commerce Committee never acted, and it died when the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Blunt Rochester introduced the bill on December 16, 2020, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the action history records only the introduction and the committee referral before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online platforms with more than 100 million users are better off: they keep using interfaces designed to maximize engagement and data collection, and keep running behavioral research on users, with no federal consent or disclosure requirement. Users of those platforms are in the same position as before.

for.name: Rep. Lisa Blunt Rochester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over consumer protection and internet policy
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.name: Large internet platforms
against.role: Operators of social media and online services with more than 100 million users
against.what_they_did: As an industry they opposed federal restrictions on dark patterns and consent requirements for behavioral research during this period; the bill was never taken up.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member of either party cosponsored the bill, so no partisan split is visible in the record; the outcome was decided by inaction in committee, not by a party-line roll call.

industries.industry: Large social media and online platforms
industries.note: Platforms with over 100 million users would have to redesign away interfaces engineered to maximize engagement and would need informed consent for behavioral experiments. Their engagement-driven, data-rich business model is exactly what the bill targets.
Consent requirements and disclosure of behavioral research would reduce the flow of user data and attention-based targeting that fuels advertising revenue on large platforms.

Firms hired by large operators to run A/B tests and behavioral studies would need informed consent, review-board approval, and periodic disclosure, raising costs and ending some opaque testing. The bill does allow FTC-defined exemptions for minor, non-manipulative preference testing.
